newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - Firmenich sniffs out Asian tastes and smells.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Firmenich sniffs out Asian tastes and smells.

text.p: Pungent, unfamiliar smells greet visitors to Firmenich Asia (Pte) Ltd's new manufacturing and development centre in Singapore.

But the odour does not bother Michel Bongi, vice president and regional manager of Firmenich Perfumery in the Asia-Pacific region, because fragrances and flavours are what the Geneva-based company creates.

A family-run company founded in 1895 by Swiss chemist Philippe Chuit, Firmenich today boasts of being the world's largest private company and the seventh largest in the fragrance and flavour industry. With about one billion Swiss francs (US$790 million) in annual sales revenue, the firm holds a seven to eight percent slice of the world's flavour and fragrance market.
"We have some targets to increase that market share through organic growth and possibly acquisition. We wish to get 10 percent by 2000," Bongi said.

Walking with evident pride through the newly renovated Singapore $10 million centre, Bongi, who has been in Singapore for five years, told Reuters about 20 to 25 percent of Firmenich's annual sales, or US$10 billion, is generated by Asia and he expects Asia's contribution to remain at those levels in the next three to four years.

"Asia is very much the focus in our corporation," Bongi said while showing one of his new creative perfume laboratories, which has two walls covered with vials of various chemicals he compares to keys on a piano.

Five "noses" or perfumers use these different "keys", some natural, some synthetic and some bulk chemicals, to create fragrances which make a lasting impression. A sophisticated weighing machine measures extracts from the vials, which are then combined in a test tube.
"Scent is a very important business. If you give two detergents of the same base but different perfumes, users will say the one with the stronger smell washes whiter. It's psychological," Bongi said.

He listed China, Japan, Indonesia and India as the company's main areas of focus in Asia. And the expansion of the Singapore office, occupying a total built-up area of 9,000 square metres, reflects this corporate commitment, he said.

The centre houses laboratories which replicate the home or working environment, such as a mini laundromat, a kitchen and a hair salon, where employees can use and test the company's latest products. The centre also has an application laboratory for flavours where food technologists or "mouths" assess flavours for drinks, sweets, savouries and dairy products.

As part of its globalisation plans, Firmenich also has a development centre in Japan, facilities in Indonesia, two manufacturing joint ventures in China's Suzhou and Kunming, and three representative offices in Shanghai, Beijing and Guangzhou in China as well as a regional office in Hong Kong.

"We are looking for opportunities. The economies in Asia are growing very fast,..with some quantum leaps. We can see markets growing five to 15 percent per annum, in some segments much more," Bongi said.

One of Firmenich's recent fragrance achievements was the contract for the creation of Calvin Klein's CK One fragrance, which was launched last year and has been a stunning retail success since. Firmenich won the contract over Swiss rival and giant Givaudan-Roure.

Its other international perfume customers include Procter & Gamble, Unilever and Colgate-Palmolive. Fine perfume clients include L'Oreal and Estee Lauder, and Nestle SA is a client on the food flavour side.

Perfume production contributes 45 percent to the company's annual turnover, chemicals contribute 20 percent and flavours make up the remainder. Bongi expects the flavour sector to grow faster than the fragrance business.
He admits there are many casualties in the perfumery business due to a limited number of department stores. Some analysts say nine out of 10 new fragrances are destined to fail.

But Bongi said the risk is lower for Firmenich Asia, which deals more with functional perfumes like those in soaps and personal care products, which have a longer life span and fewer new entries than the fine perfume business.
The company plans to stay on top of competition through innovation, creativity and customer service, which Bongi believes help the company live up to its motto of "making things irresistible".
